title: EnquiryOS — Revenue Incident Response for the Agentic Web
pitch: Browser agents find missed revenue, inspect the evidence, rank recovery, draft a response, and stage it for explicit human approval through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Browser agents find missed revenue, inspect the evidence, rank recovery, draft a response, and stage it for explicit human approval through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inbound businesses do not always lose revenue because they lack leads. They lose it when a genuine enquiry gets buried, a follow-up is missed, or nobody realizes that a high-intent customer is still waiting. Most sales software focuses on acquiring, organizing, or generating leads. We wanted to explore a different question: What revenue has the business already paid to acquire — but quietly failed to recover? EnquiryOS is our answer: Revenue Incident Response for the Agentic Web. A Revenue Incident is a point where observed customer intent and the business response diverge in a way that may have caused recoverable loss. The product is deliberately not a generic CRM, chatbot, or autonomous sales agent. It is an evidence-backed recovery layer that lets a browser agent investigate what was missed while keeping consequential action under explicit human control. What it does EnquiryOS exposes five semantic WebMCP tools directly from the web application: audit_missed_enquiries inspect_enquiry_evidence rank_recovery_queue draft_recovery_message prepare_recovery Together they form a complete recovery workflow: Audit → Inspect evidence → Rank → Draft → Stage → Human commits An agent can ask EnquiryOS what the business may have missed, inspect the evidence behind a Revenue Incident, understand why one incident ranks above another, produce an evidence-grounded recovery draft, and stage it for approval. There is deliberately no agent-callable send tool . The authority boundary is: Observe → Investigate → Reason → Propose → Stage → Human commits This means the browser agent can do the investigative and preparatory work, but the final consequential action remains with the person operating the business. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with a web application generally has to infer intent from visual structure and operate through brittle UI actions. EnquiryOS instead exposes explicit semantic capabilities through document.modelContext . The agent does not need to guess that a particular button means "find missed enquiries" or scrape the page to understand the recovery queue. It can invoke a purpose-built tool such as audit_missed_enquiries , receive structured evidence, and immediately see the corresponding state reflected in the application's visible interface. The tool calls and the human interface share the same application state. Every WebMCP action also appears in a visible Live Trace, so the human can see what the agent has done. That creates a much stronger human-agent interaction model: the agent investigates, EnquiryOS provides the evidence, and the human retains authority. The demo The demo follows one Revenue Incident involving Ananya Sharma. Her incoming message asks about Saturday availability and package options. EnquiryOS identifies that there was no subsequent business reply and that the wait exceeded the service target. The incident is marked confirmed , with 97% evidence confidence , and receives a deterministic recovery score of 96/100 . Importantly, the score is not presented as an unexplained AI judgment. EnquiryOS shows the evidence signals that produced the priority: high-value enquiry; strong evidence confidence; an explicit availability question; no outbound reply; service-target breach. The agent can then generate a recovery draft grounded in that inspected evidence. Finally, prepare_recovery moves the incident into Awaiting approval . At that point the agent stops. The human sees the checkpoint and retains the only action capable of committing the recovery. How we built it EnquiryOS is a focused Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. The WebMCP integration uses native document.modelContext.registerTool registrations with structured input schemas, tool descriptions, and explicit behavioral boundaries. The five tools operate on a deterministic synthetic enquiry dataset so the judging experience is reproducible and the evidence chain can be inspected consistently. The interface contains three synchronized views: a Revenue Incident recovery queue; an evidence and recovery workspace; a Live Trace of agent tool activity. The recovery score is deterministic rather than generated by an opaque model. Drafts are also constrained by the evidence associated with the selected incident. We intentionally did not embed a proprietary LLM inside EnquiryOS for this prototype. The reasoning agent comes from the browser/user environment; EnquiryOS provides the domain-specific tools, evidence and shared state that make that agent useful. Challenges we faced One of the most interesting challenges was making the boundary between agent capability and human authority part of the product architecture rather than merely a warning in the interface. It would have been easy to add another WebMCP tool called send_message . We deliberately did not. Instead, the most powerful agent-callable operation is prepare_recovery , which may stage a draft but cannot commit it. We also had to make the WebMCP lifecycle robust inside React, ensure the five registrations remained stable across component lifecycle behavior, keep server/client rendering deterministic, and ensure that state-mutating tool responses returned the newly prepared state rather than stale pre-mutation data. The result is a deterministic WebMCP workflow that remains visible and understandable to the human throughout the interaction. What we learned The most important lesson was that agentic interfaces become more useful when websites expose domain intent , not just clickable surfaces. A tool called inspect_enquiry_evidence carries far more meaning than an instruction to click a card, scroll down, and read several DOM nodes. We also learned that agent safety does not necessarily mean reducing capability. EnquiryOS gives the agent significant investigative power while making its authority ceiling explicit. That separation — powerful investigation, evidence-bound reasoning, and human-controlled commitment — is the model we would like to carry forward as agent-enabled websites become more common. What's next The prototype currently uses deterministic synthetic enquiry data. The next step is connecting the same WebMCP recovery layer to real business systems such as inboxes, CRMs, WhatsApp-style enquiry channels, web forms, and booking systems. From there, EnquiryOS can learn organization-specific recovery policies, measure whether staged recoveries actually convert, and identify recurring leakage patterns across channels. The larger vision is simple: Find revenue the business may have missed. Prove why it was missed. Recover what still matters. And let the agent do the investigation without taking authority away from the human.
